transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-28 15:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park, Priya Singh, Marcus Lee (Redwood); Daniel Ortiz, Maya Chen, Arjun Rao, Leah Gomez (Vellum)

Summary:
Quick sync on POC results from last week's tuning: focused on function/tool-calling reliability, structured JSON output stability, and runtime latency with different batching configs. Agreement to run a dedicated 3-day benchmark and exchange canonical prompts + schemas. Action items and timeline captured at the end.

Agenda:
- Quick wins from last week
- SDK invoke patterns and function-calling reliability
- Structured output failures and mitigation patterns
- Runtime tuning: batching, kv-cache, quantization tradeoffs
- Security/ops notes and next steps

Transcript body:
00:00 Ethan Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll try to keep to 45 minutes, quick status then deep dive on the new invoke traces Priya shared.
00:11 Daniel Ortiz: yep thanks Ethan, morning from our side, lots to cover. Maya and Arjun on the line as well.
00:18 Priya Singh: cool, I pushed the instrumented logs into the shared folder, there's a csv with per-request latencies and a separate json with function-calling failures. note: some timestamps got shifted due to beacon sampler so small offset.
00:31 Maya Chen: saw that — the failure rate looked low but consistent around 2-3% for multi-invoke flows. interested in the root cause.
00:39 Marcus Lee: yeah we dug in, two main patterns: one was schema mismatch where the model attempted to return partial JSON and we timed out; second was a KV cache eviction scenario for long sessions that caused extra decoding cost.
00:53 Arjun Rao: when you say timeout, what's the threshold you used in the SDK? we currently set client timeout to 8s per chunk.
01:02 Priya Singh: we used server-side SLO of 6s p50-ish for short sequences, but allowed 12s on long sequences during the test; the client 8s probably clipped a few responses causing aborts.
01:12 Leah Gomez: that aligns with what we saw in product — sometimes UI shows spinner then blank result.
01:18 Ethan Park: ok first follow up — we recommend aligning client timeout to server SLO plus a safety buffer, so for your current workload set to 15 seconds while we tune batching. that should reduce the aborts caused by client-side cutoffs.
01:33 Daniel Ortiz: makes sense; what's the cause of schema partials though? is it hallucination or streaming chunk boundary issues?
01:40 Priya Singh: a bit of both. we observed two classes: a) model produced truncated JSON due to early stop when token budget exhausted, and b) streaming chunk boundary cut the JSON mid-atom — the SDK's reassembly logic attempted to concat chunks but didn't validate full JSON structure.
01:56 Marcus Lee: important point: with function-calling we ask model to return a JSON object representing method and args. if the output is chunked we need to run a robust final-assembly step + schema validation before invoking downstream tools.
02:08 Maya Chen: do you have a recommended validator or should we run our existing JSON schema?
02:13 Priya Singh: use your schema but add a final model output validator in the client that retries an auto-heal: one more regenerate with a focused prompt like 'The last response was malformed; please return valid JSON matching X schema' then micro-retry up to 2 times. we saw that recover about 60% of malformed outputs.
02:30 Arjun Rao: micro-retries sound fine but we'd worry about cost. any heuristics when to retry versus fallback?
02:36 Priya Singh: if the model produced a near-JSON (we saw 1-2 missing brackets or trailing commas) do a single focused retry. if completely unrecognizable, fallback to human review pathway per your SLA. Also caching: if similar prompt produced valid output in last 10 minutes, prefer cached.
02:52 Ethan Park: switching gears to runtime tuning — Priya, can you summarize the batching experiments?
02:58 Priya Singh: sure. we ran 3 configs: 1) conservative small batches (batch size ~4, concurrency high) optimized for latency; 2) aggressive batching (batch size ~32) for throughput; 3) adaptive batching with sequence-length histograms where short sequences batch up to 16, long sequences isolated. results: conservative had median latency 180ms on short seqs but high cost; aggressive had p95 blowouts for short interactive requests; adaptive was best tradeoff — p50 ~220ms and cost down ~18%.
03:27 Daniel Ortiz: can you share the histogram you used? our distribution is very spiky — ~70% < 32 tokens, 20% 32-512, 10% >512.
03:36 Priya Singh: yes that's exactly what we saw similar to your numbers. adaptive batching uses two lanes: fast lane for <=64 tokens and slow lane for longer. also we used prefix caching for repeated starts which saved ~12% tokens.
03:49 Maya Chen: prefix caching — was that on the Redwood side or in our app?
03:53 Marcus Lee: Redwood runtime supports KV cache for prefix reuse, but you can also cache client-side; we recommend letting runtime handle KV cache when you have multi-tenant reuse patterns, since it can manage eviction across requests. But for deterministic fragments, client-side cache is fine.
04:07 Arjun Rao: the KV cache eviction issue you mentioned earlier, what caused it?
04:11 Priya Singh: two causes: oversized session windows (we held KV state for sessions >30 min) and memory pressure on the instance during long benchmarks. we changed eviction policy to LRU with session TTL 10 minutes and that dropped evictions during normal loads.
04:26 Daniel Ortiz: good. about quantization — you mentioned potential quality regressions at 4-bit for some of our models?
04:32 Marcus Lee: yes, quantization reduces memory/cost but can slightly affect generation fidelity particularly for instruction-heavy prompts. for your safety-critical extraction flows we recommend 8-bit or Q4_K_M profiles and run regression evals on your canonical prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant config per-prompt set.
04:52 Leah Gomez: security quick point — we need SOC2 evidence and details on KMS integration for customer-managed keys. Maya raised this earlier.
04:59 Ethan Park: I'll send the security pack, but quick notes: Redwood Private supports customer KMS (AES + HSM) for on-prem and VPC. Hosted can integrate with customer KMS for encryption-in-transit and at-rest but we need an enterprise contract for managed keys. Action: I'll share the SOC2 report and KMS integration doc.
05:16 Maya Chen: perfect. also, on function-calling — we want to ensure the SDK doesn't auto-execute a tool if the returned JSON is slightly off. is there a safety gate?
05:24 Priya Singh: yes the SDK has an execution hook that accepts a validator callback. default is conservative: it will not auto-run if schema validation fails. you can customize to auto-heal + re-validate.
05:34 Arjun Rao: what about retries for tool invocation timeouts? if downstream tool is flaky we risk duplicate side-effects.
05:40 Marcus Lee: we recommend idempotency keys and two-phase commit patterns. the SDK supports attaching an idempotency token to each tool call and provides a 'dry-run-validate' mode to confirm intent before execution.
05:54 Daniel Ortiz: great. let's talk about observability — those per-route dashboards look useful but we need trace-level debugging for a specific failed session. can we pull request-level logs?
06:04 Priya Singh: yes, Redwood Console stores per-request traces for the retention window of your plan. For Dedicated pilot we'll enable extended retention and allow you to download raw traces. We'll share a link to a sample trace format.
06:16 Leah Gomez: sample link please.
06:18 Ethan Park: will include with the security pack, along with an explainer.
06:23 Maya Chen: ok next — structured output stability. We tried to use function-calling for multi-step extraction: first extract entities, then call reranker tool, then format final JSON. We saw occasional ordering issues where reranker returned before entities were stable.
06:38 Priya Singh: ordering can be enforced by explicit sync points: use function-calling for 'extract_entities' with a strict response schema, validate, then call 'rerank' as a separate transaction. If you embed both in one call you save one round trip but increase fragility. For mission-critical flows, prefer small atomic calls.
06:56 Arjun Rao: any guidance on token budgets when chaining multiple function calls?
07:01 Marcus Lee: budget per chain: estimate worst-case token expansion from intermediate steps and reserve by setting 'max_total_tokens' on the session. Redwood runtime supports per-session token caps and will enforce gracefully with an error code you can handle.
07:15 Daniel Ortiz: let's discuss the proposed dedicated benchmark. specifics?
07:20 Priya Singh: propose 72-hour window with three phases: phase A baseline (hosted default configs), phase B adaptive batching + prefix cache, phase C dedicated GPU pool with quantization profile Q4_K_M and increased KV cache TTL. We'll measure p50/p95 latency, token cost, and function-calling success rate.
07:38 Maya Chen: can we include our production-like traffic shape? bursts up to 500 RPS for short windows.
07:44 Priya Singh: yes we'll replay recorded traffic; we need a sanitized sample from you — remove PII and provide 1 hour of representative traffic to scale to your expected peak.
07:55 Ethan Park: timeline: Priya runs initial warm-up tests next week, full 72-hour run start 2026-11-09 pending data handoff.
08:03 Daniel Ortiz: sounds good. Leah: product concerns?
08:07 Leah Gomez: two things — UX fallback messaging for malformed outputs, and analytics hooks to measure end-to-end success. we'll coordinate with Maya.
08:14 Maya Chen: I'll add telemetry events: output_valid, output_repaired, output_fallback.
08:19 Arjun Rao: Ops note: network latency to Redwood region is ~80ms from our staging region, could be 30-40ms in prod. we'll test.
08:26 Marcus Lee: that's fine; our routing can prefer nearest region when using Dedicated in cloud provider X.
08:33 Daniel Ortiz: competitors — we also evaluated Anthropic's tool-calling but their function schema rigidity caused integration overhead. Vertex had good throughput but their billing granularity didn't line up with our cost model.
08:48 Ethan Park: quick risks: cost vs latency tradeoffs when enabling micro-retries and adaptive batching. we'll provide cost estimates for each phase.
08:55 Priya Singh: one more operational tip: enable deterministic seed for evaluation runs to compare outputs across quantization profiles. that will surface regressions reliably.
09:05 Maya Chen: good call.
09:08 Ethan Park: ok wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners?
09:12 Daniel Ortiz: sure go ahead.
09:14 Ethan Park: Priya to share tuned batching config + histogram (by 2026-11-02), Priya to run the 72-hour dedicated benchmark and publish raw logs (due 2026-11-09 report 11-12), Maya to upload canonical prompts/schema (due 2026-11-04), Arjun to run latency tests (due 2026-11-03), Ethan to send security pack and pricing (due 2026-11-01).
09:41 Leah Gomez: we'll review and schedule the benchmark start once we confirm sanitized traffic handoff.
09:48 Daniel Ortiz: thanks all.
09:50 Ethan Park: thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with links and calendar for the benchmark start.

End of transcript.
